Neonatal Beluga whales, Delphinapterus leucas, emerge from the womb at a modest size given the immense proportions they will eventually attain.
Calves typically measure approximately 130 centimeters [Lb = approximately 130 centimeters] at birth, a length that facilitates passage through the birth canal while still allowing sufficient mass for thermoregulation in Arctic waters.
Newborn individuals enter the world weighing about 60,000 grams [Wwb = about 60,000 grams], a substantial neonatal mass that supports rapid early development in the frigid estuarine environments where calving occurs.
This initial investment in offspring size is typical of cetaceans, which produce relatively large, precocial neonates capable of swimming immediately after parturition.
The birth weight provides the calf with enough blubber reserves to maintain thermal homeostasis while it learns to nurse and navigate the dense, cold waters of its natal habitat.

Sexual dimorphism in body size is pronounced in this species, with adult males considerably larger than their female counterparts, reflecting the polygynous mating system observed in many odontocetes.
Females achieve an ultimate total length of approximately 370 centimeters [Li = approximately 370 centimeters], whereas males continue growing to a substantially greater asymptotic length of 440 centimeters [Li = 440 centimeters].
This disparity in final body size is accompanied by a corresponding difference in ultimate wet weight: adult females reach a maximum body mass of about 950,000 grams [Wwi = about 950,000 grams], a value derived from allometric scaling relationships predicting that a smaller-bodied adult will weigh proportionally less than a larger one.
In contrast, adult males can attain an ultimate wet weight of 1,600,000 grams [Wwi = 1,600,000 grams], making them one of the heavier Arctic cetaceans and conferring advantages in male-male competition during the breeding season, where larger individuals are better able to monopolize access to receptive females.

The reproductive chronology of Belugas follows a pattern typical of long-lived, slow-reproducing marine mammals, with several key milestones measured relative to the time of birth under the species' normal core body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C].
Gestation in Delphinapterus leucas lasts 416 days [tg = 416 days], a prolonged period that allows for extensive fetal development and the deposition of sufficient blubber for neonatal survival in cold waters at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C].
After parturition, the calf remains dependent on maternal milk for a considerable duration, with weaning occurring at 679 days since birth [tx = 679 days since birth], a protracted nursing period that facilitates the gradual transition to solid prey such as fish and invertebrates while the young animal develops foraging competence and builds the thick blubber layer necessary for independent thermoregulation at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C].
This extended maternal investment is characteristic of cetaceans, where learning complex foraging techniques in variable Arctic habitats requires substantial time under maternal guidance.

Puberty in both sexes is attained well after the weaning period, reflecting the need for considerable somatic growth before reproductive onset.
Females reach sexual maturity at 1,644 days since birth [tp = 1,644 days since birth], while males, despite their larger ultimate size, reach puberty later at 2,283 days since birth [tp = 2,283 days since birth], all measured against the species' internal body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C].
This sex-specific difference in maturation timing is intriguing: despite achieving a smaller adult body size, females require roughly 1.5 years less time to become reproductively viable than males do to begin producing sperm.
The later maturation in males likely relates to the competitive advantages of large body size in securing breeding opportunities, as smaller males would be at a significant disadvantage during aggressive interactions for access to estrous females.
Consequently, the onset of gametogenesis in males is deferred until they have reached a size that allows them to compete effectively.

Longevity records for Belugas indicate a maximum lifespan of 60 years [am = 60 years] for females studied at the core body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a duration that places them among the longer-lived Arctic cetaceans.
Males, by contrast, tend to have shorter lifespans, likely due to the energetic costs and physical injuries associated with intrasexual competition during the breeding season.
Given this extended lifespan and the protracted period until sexual maturity, the species exhibits a low maximum reproductive rate: an individual female can produce approximately 1 calf every 0.3 years [Ri = approximately 1 calf every 0.3 years] under optimal conditions, a high-frequency interval for a cetacean of this size.
This translates to a theoretical maximum of about 3 calves per year if continuous breeding were possible, though in practice, the energetic demands of gestation and lactation likely impose longer interbirth intervals in free-ranging populations inhabiting the resource-variable Arctic ecosystem.
